content: This report provides updated recommendations for the prevention and control of hantavirus infections associated with rodents in the United States. It replaces the previous report published by the CDC in 1993. The recommendations are based on principles of rodent and infection control, as well as evidence indicating that most infections result from exposure to infected rodents in enclosed spaces. In 1993, a previously unknown disease, hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), was identified among residents of the southwestern United States. HPS has since been recognized throughout the contiguous United States and the Americas. Hantaviruses are associated with rodent reservoirs, necessitating measures to minimize human exposure to wild rodents. These recommendations are informed by the current understanding of the epidemiology of hantavirus infections in the United States. Rodent Reservoirs of Viruses Causing HPS All hantaviruses known to cause HPS are carried by New World rats and mice, specifically those in the family Muridae, subfamily Sigmodontinae. This subfamily includes at least 430 species of mice and rats, which are widespread in North and South America. Unlike urban rodents such as house mice and Norway rats, these wild rodents are more commonly found in rural and suburban areas. Certain species, such as the deer mouse (Peromyscus maniculatus) and the white-footed mouse (Peromyscus leucopus), may enter human habitations in these areas. The deer mouse is the primary host for Sin Nombre virus (SNV), the main causative agent of HPS in the United States. Deer mice are common and widely distributed in rural areas across much of the country. On average, approximately 10% of deer mice tested show evidence of infection with SNV. Other hantaviruses associated with sigmodontine rodents and known to cause HPS include the New York virus (hosted by the white-footed mouse), Black Creek Canal virus (hosted by the cotton rat), and Bayou virus (hosted by the rice rat). Nearly all of the continental United States falls within the range of one or more of these host species. Several other sigmodontine rodent species in the United States are associated with additional hantaviruses that have not yet been implicated in human disease. These include the brush mouse (Peromyscus boylii) and the Western harvest mouse (Reithrodontomys megalotis). Only the deer mouse and the white-footed mouse are commonly associated with peridomestic environments. Identifying characteristics and natural histories of these host species are available from other sources. Numerous sigmodontine rodent species are also associated with HPS in South America. New sigmodontine hantavirus hosts are discovered each year, and more are likely to be identified. Until the full extent of hantavirus infection and pathogenicity among sigmodontine species is understood, it is recommended to treat all sigmodontine rodents as potential hosts of HPS-causing hantaviruses. For the general public, this recommendation applies to all wild mice and rats encountered in rural areas throughout the United States. Other Diseases Associated with Hantavirus Infection HPS is restricted to the Americas because sigmodontine rodents are limited to this region. In contrast, another group of hantaviruses associated with murine and arvicoline rodents causes hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Europe and Asia. Hantaan and Dobrava viruses, hosted by murine field mice, cause thousands of severe HFRS cases annually in Asia and Eastern Europe, with fatality rates as high as 10%. The Norway rat is the host for Seoul virus, which causes a milder form of HFRS in Asia. Evidence of Seoul virus infection has been found in Norway rats worldwide, including in the United States, but human disease caused by this virus is largely restricted to Asia. Puumala virus, carried by the bank vole, causes a mild form of HFRS known as nephropathia epidemica (NE), which is common in northern Europe and has a case fatality rate of less than 1%. Several other arvicoline rodent species host hantaviruses in the northern hemisphere, including the United States, but none have been associated with human disease. Infection in the Host Hantaviruses do not cause overt illness in their rodent hosts. Infected rodents shed the virus in saliva, urine, and feces for weeks, months, or even for life. The quantity of virus shed is highest approximately 3–8 weeks after infection. The presence of infectious virus in rodent saliva and the sensitivity of these animals to hantaviruses following intramuscular inoculation suggest that biting may be an important mode of transmission among rodents. Field data indicate that transmission occurs horizontally, more frequently among male rodents, and may be associated with fighting. Although other mammals can become infected after contact with infected rodents, there is no evidence that these dead-end hosts can transmit the virus to other animals or humans. However, domestic animals such as cats and dogs may bring infected rodents into contact with humans. Arthropod vectors are not known to play a role in hantavirus transmission. Transmission to Humans Hantaviruses are primarily transmitted to humans through the inhalation of infectious, aerosolized saliva or excreta. Transmission can also occur when contaminated materials are disturbed and inhaled, introduced into broken skin or mucous membranes, or ingested in contaminated food or water. Human infections have been reported after rodent bites. High-risk activities include entering or cleaning rodent-infested structures, handling rodents without gloves, and disturbing rodent nests or excreta. Person-to-person transmission has not been associated with Old World hantaviruses or HPS cases in the United States. However, nosocomial transmission of Andes virus was documented during an outbreak in Argentina and suspected in another outbreak in Chile. Epidemiology Hantavirus infections are associated with activities that bring humans into contact with infected rodents, usually in rural settings. HPS cases in the United States occur throughout the year, with higher numbers reported in spring and summer. Known risk factors include increasing numbers of host rodents in human dwellings, cleaning rodent-infested structures, and handling equipment or machinery stored in rodent-infested areas. The absolute risk of hantavirus infection to the general public in North America is low, with only 20–50 HPS cases confirmed annually in the United States since 1993. Prevention Eradicating rodent hosts of hantaviruses is neither feasible nor desirable due to their ecological importance. The best approach for disease prevention is risk reduction through environmental modification and hygiene practices that deter rodents from colonizing human environments. Safe cleanup of rodent waste and nesting materials is also essential. Simple and inexpensive methods have been shown to effectively prevent rodents from entering rural dwellings. Precautions to Limit Exposure Rodent control in and around the home is the primary strategy for preventing hantavirus infection. Homes should be inspected regularly for openings that could allow rodent entry. If evidence of infestation is detected, precautions should be taken to reduce rodent shelter and food sources and to prevent entry through rodent-proofing measures. Traps should be used cautiously, and gloves should be worn when handling rodents or traps. For outdoor areas, woodpiles and other materials should be stored away from the home, and food sources that attract rodents should be removed. Trash should be disposed of in rodent-proof containers, and dense vegetation near the home should be cleared. Occupational and Recreational Precautions Workers frequently exposed to rodents, such as mammalogists and pest-control workers, are at higher risk for hantavirus infection and should take enhanced precautions, including the use of respiratory protection and gloves. Campers and hikers should avoid contact with rodents and their nests, use rodent-proof food storage, and avoid sleeping on the ground.
